explanation: Fires strongly in file-preamble code boilerplate: the package segment after 'android' in import lines (android[[.app]], [[.util]]), '.h' in #include <stdlib.h>, '<html' after DOCTYPE, and Rust attribute '#['. It also fires at ~80% on a scattered set of unrelated prose tokens (mid-word pieces of names, 'barrister', 'app'). Ordinary prose is weak.

Decision-making phrases: fires on 'make'/'making' when the object is decisions/choices ('to make informed choices', 'must make decisions', 'in making clinical decisions'), and on the adjective before 'decision' ('the right/wrong/crucial decision'). Weaker on other words in decision contexts ('before committing', 'the decision'); 'make' without a decision sense is weak.

Fires on the head noun that completes a noun phrase introduced by a determiner or modifier, mostly in technical, Q&A or academic setup text ('using a [[link]]', 'the below [[trigger]] code', 'the following [[statements]]', 'common [[proofs]]', 'VF [[rhythm]]'). Generic concrete nouns in everyday prose fire weakly.

A mixture centred on numbers and counting: the second minus in arithmetic 'x - -y', ordinal and count words ('second season', 'three straight', 'final quarter', 'one Western Harvest Mouse'), digits in citations and section labels, plus some unrelated tokens (include paths, 'Dad', 'early').

Prepositions and verbs that link a patient or object to a clinical encounter or detection method in medical case and scientific writing: 'presented [[to]]', 'admitted/referred [[to]] our hospital', 'detected [[by]] palpation', 'lesion [[on]] angiography', 'while [[receiving]] drug', 'screening [[via]]'. The same prepositions in non-clinical text are weak to moderate.

A heterogeneous mix: code syntax tokens (nested 'namespace', the ':' in 'xmlns:android', '!' in '+build !gccgo', config file names), the decimal point or digit in percentages inside parentheses ('(0[[.]]7%)'), and assorted prose words ('these', 'commercial', 'number').

Fires on the second or closing token of a familiar multi-word expression or name, where the token is highly predictable from what comes before ('ten years [[ago]]', 'slam [[dunk]]', 'print [[archive]]', 'animal [[welfare]]', 'Harvard-M[[IT]]', 'Nag[[oya]]'). The examples are varied and don't form a tight semantic group.

Fires on interior subword pieces of words split into several tokens, mainly non-English or foreign proper names ('neg[[oc]]ia', 'Alg[[ern]]on', 'Liebk[[ne]]cht', 'Kam[[al]]', 'Sud[[bury]]', German, Norwegian and Hungarian words). Whole common English words fire weakly or not at all.

A mixture of predictable continuation tokens: 'year' in 'this year's / earlier this year' (the most consistent), the suffix in tech names ('ASP[[.NET]]', 'ember[[js]]', 'Google[[+]]', '<[[linux]]/'), and words like 'every [[single]]', 'this [[latter]]', 'Breaking [[Bad]]'.

Fires on the head noun of a compound or modifier-noun phrase, mostly in scientific or technical text ('K+ [[current]]', 'IC [[chip]]', 'SMS [[messages]]', 'actin [[mRNA]]', 'trait test anxiety'), and strongly on 'House' as a word start (House Speaker, Households, Housewives). Also some mid-word pieces of names and terms.

Two related jobs. (1) The suffix pieces that complete technical or medical words ('RIJNDA[[EL]]', 'plasmin[[ogen]]', 'rivarox[[aban]]', 'cut[[aneous]]', 'erythropo[[iet]]in'). (2) The predictable word in stock phrases ('the U.S. state [[of]]', 'Apache [[License]]', 'the success [[of]]'). Both are completions of a highly predictable fixed term.

A mix of tokens that complete a predictable phrase in many genres: names ('Clap[[ton]]', 'NSCL[[C]]', 'Dawson'), legal and contract wording ('We [[grant]] the motion', 'have the [[meaning]]', 'a copy [[of]] the GNU'), code ('public [[void]]', '// [[Do]] any additional setup'). There is no shared semantic theme.

Fires on the first token (often a single capital letter) of a capitalized proper name or abbreviation that is split into several tokens, especially at the start of a name after a space or newline ('[[L]]'Orchestra', '[[L]].A.', '[[D]].C.', '[[L]]UBBOCK', '[[R]]AILROAD', '[[T]]enth Circuit', '[[D]]ikembe'). Later pieces of the name are weak.

Mainly closing-tag tokens in markup ('', ''). It also fires on unrelated tokens such as the comma after a date ('June 6[[,]]'), statement terminators in code (';', '");'), and random mid-word or prose tokens.

A heterogeneous set: 'referred [[to]]', 'P[[open]]', the space between date or score fields in tables ('5-10 [[ ]]20:0'), 'The [[aim]] of this paper', mid-word pieces of foreign-language text (Japanese, Russian, Finnish, Dutch), and the comma in company names.

A mixture of tokens in coordination or noun-phrase completions ('alone [[or]] with', 'one conventional [[and]] two', 'one [[object]]', 'a new [[location]]', 'copyright [[notice]]', 'moving [[average]]'). It has no clear single trigger.

The opening parenthesis ' (' that starts a parenthetical aside after a noun phrase in prose: biographical dates after a person's full name ('Derek Henry Junior Duncan [[(]]born'), 'e.g.'/'i.e.' asides, abbreviations, legal and license text ('DAMAGES (INCLUDING', 'files (the "Software")'). Parentheses in code, function calls or formulas fire weakly.

Fires most strongly on the verb in purpose or infinitive constructions such as 'to [[bring]]/[[make]]/[[put]]' and 'toward [[bringing]]' (bring something about, make something happen). It also fires on an unrelated set: 'x' in '4x100m', 'typename' in C++, the colon in clock times, include-path components, and German or Dutch auxiliaries.

The word 'the' in fixed boilerplate or name-like contexts: '([[the]] "License")' in Apache headers, 'published by [[the]] Free Software Foundation', 'The use/contents of this file' in license headers, 'the' as part of a URL domain ('www.[[the]]atlantic.com', 'thehill'), and 'Search The Blog'. Ordinary 'the' in running prose is weak to moderate (20-30%).

A mix: legal case captions (the line break after party names, 'UNITED STATES of [[America]]'), 'this country' and similar national or organizational references ('the [[party]]', 'Lady [[Bears]]'), plus URL path pieces and assorted name fragments.

There is no coherent pattern: medical and biological word pieces ('at[[ax]]ia', 'acid[[uria]]', 'FT[[D]]'), code tokens ('cb', 'type'), German, and assorted common words ('orbit', 'audit', 'then', 'would', 'cars').
